lines.text: A small island in the Gulf that has lived by trade for five thousand years, from ancient Dilmun to pearls and oil. This is Bahrain.
About five thousand years ago Bahrain was Dilmun, a land of merchants standing between Mesopotamia and the Indus.
At Qal'at al-Bahrain, city was built upon city for four thousand years, and a Portuguese fort crowns the mound today.
By the thirteen hundreds Manama had grown up on the coast, the town that would become the capital.
In 1783 the Al Khalifa family took the islands, and they have ruled them ever since, while pearls were the wealth of the Gulf.
Then came oil. In 1932 the Bahrain Petroleum Company struck the first oil on the Arab side of the Gulf.
Isa bin Salman Al Khalifa would become emir in 1961, and lead his country to independence.
His son, Hamad, would succeed him in 1999, and a few years later take the title of king.
In 1971 Bahrain left British protection and became an independent state.
Work began on a causeway to Saudi Arabia, and when it opened in 1986 the island was joined to the mainland by road.
In 2004 Bahrain held the first Formula One race in the Middle East.
In 2011, in the Arab Spring, crowds filled the streets of Manama, and the protests were put down with Saudi help.
In 2012 the old pearling trail of Muharraq, its merchants' houses and oyster beds, was named a World Heritage Site.
And in 2020 Bahrain signed the Abraham Accords, setting up ties with Israel.
Dilmun's merchants, the pearl divers and the oil men all made their living from the same small island.
